title: Text types and organizational structures
blurb: Name a passage's text type and its overall organizational structure from how the ideas connect, not from a single signal word.
question: A passage begins, “The first effect was felt within weeks,” and goes on to explain how one clinic's closing led to longer emergency room waits. Is it organized by sequence or by cause and effect, and how can you be sure?

teach.body: Every passage has a text type (what kind of writing it is) and an organizational structure (how its ideas are arranged). The five text types are narrative, expository, persuasive or argumentative, descriptive and technical. Structure is the pattern linking the ideas: time order, causes and effects, comparisons, problems and solutions, and so on. Plain English: type is the genre; structure is the skeleton.

head: Structure
Signal words
Fits
rows: because, therefore, as a result, leads to
types, kinds, categories, is defined as

teach.h: Judge the whole, not one word
teach.body: Signal words are clues, but one word does not set the structure. “First” can appear in a cause-and-effect passage; “however” can appear in a problem-and-solution passage. Ask what question the whole passage answers. In what order did things happen? Why did it happen? How are these alike or different? What is wrong and how can it be fixed? The question the passage answers names its structure.

Grace, a nursing applicant, reads: “In 2022, Millbrook's only urgent care center closed. The first effect was felt within weeks: patients with sprains and sore throats began going to the hospital emergency room instead. Because the ER was treating so many minor cases, average waits rose from 40 minutes to 95. Those longer waits, in turn, led some patients to leave before they were seen at all.”

items: Notice “first” is a trap: it introduces the first effect in a chain, not a step in a process.
Ask what the passage answers: why did ER waits rise and patients leave?
Trace the links: closing caused more ER visits; more visits caused longer waits; longer waits caused walkouts.
Name it: a chain of causes and effects. The text type is expository.

teach.caption: Each box causes the next. A causal chain like this is the cause-and-effect structure, even though the events are also in time order.

teach.text: The classic trap is naming a structure from one signal word. A passage that says “first” once is not automatically sequence, and one “however” does not make a whole passage compare and contrast. Read for the relationship that runs through all the paragraphs.

items: Text types: narrative, expository, persuasive/argumentative, descriptive, technical.
Structures: sequence, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, description/spatial, order of importance, classification.
Signal words point to a structure but do not decide it alone.
Ask what question the whole passage answers.
Structure matches purpose: sequence narrates, problem-solution often persuades, classification informs.

summary: You can now identify the five text types and the seven common organizational structures. You can also name a passage's overall structure from the relationship running through it, rather than from a single signal word.

A.q: Which group of signal words most strongly suggests a compare-and-contrast structure?
A.why: “Similarly” and “both” signal likenesses, and “whereas” signals a difference. Together they mark compare and contrast.

whyNot.0: These signal a sequence or chronological order.

A.q: “The Riverside Free Clinic opened in 1998 in a church basement with two volunteer nurses. In 2004, it moved into a storefront on Main Street. Five years later, a state grant paid for a dental suite. Today, the clinic serves about 6,000 patients a year.” Which organizational structure does the passage use?
A.why: The dates (1998, 2004, five years later, today) trace the clinic's history in time order. That is a chronological structure.

whyNot.0: The passage does not explain why one event caused the next; it lists milestones in order.
whyNot.2: No problem is stated and no fix is proposed.
whyNot.3: The passage tracks changes over time rather than describing the clinic's features.

A.q: Which text type best describes a set of numbered steps for assembling a portable wheelchair ramp, with a parts list and safety warnings?
A.why: Numbered steps, specifications and warnings are the features of a technical text.

whyNot.0: Descriptive texts use sensory detail to portray a subject, not instructions.
whyNot.1: Narratives tell a story with characters and events.
whyNot.3: Persuasive texts argue for a position; assembly steps make no claim.

B.q: “Many patients at the Hillcrest clinic forgot to take their evening medications. To solve this problem, the clinic tested a text-message reminder service. After three months, missed doses dropped by a third, and the clinic now offers the service to every patient.” Which structure best describes the passage?
B.why: The passage states a problem (forgotten doses), presents a fix (text reminders) and reports that the fix worked.

whyNot.1: Nothing is compared; the passage follows one clinic's response.
whyNot.2: No categories or types are defined.
whyNot.3: A result is mentioned, but the passage is built around a problem and the action taken to fix it.

B.q: “Applicants weigh many factors when choosing a nursing program. Location matters to some, and tuition to others. More important is the quality of a program's clinical placements. Above all, though, applicants should check how many graduates pass the licensing exam.” Which structure does the passage use?
B.why: The factors build from less important (location, tuition) to “more important” to “above all.” That is order of importance.

whyNot.1: “Though” appears once, but the factors are ranked rather than compared point by point.
whyNot.2: No time order is given; the factors are ranked, not dated.
whyNot.3: The passage ranks factors by importance rather than sorting them into defined categories.

B.q: “Hospital volunteers fall into three main categories. Patient-support volunteers deliver books and keep patients company. Clerical volunteers file records and answer phones. Event volunteers staff health fairs and fundraisers.” Which structure does the passage use?
B.why: The passage sorts volunteers into “three main categories” and defines each one. That is classification.

whyNot.0: The passage sorts people into groups rather than describing one subject's features in detail.
whyNot.1: The categories are not steps or events in order.

C.q: “Two common ways to prepare for the TEAS are self-paced apps and in-person classes. Apps let students practice whenever they have a spare moment, which suits those working full-time. Classes, on the other hand, follow a fixed schedule, but they offer an instructor who can answer questions on the spot. Both cover all four test sections. The first option usually costs less, whereas the second offers more accountability.” Which best describes the passage's overall structure?
C.why: The whole passage sets two study options side by side: their differences (“on the other hand,” “whereas”) and similarities (“Both”). That is compare and contrast.

whyNot.0: “The first option” refers to the first of two choices, not the first step in a sequence.
whyNot.1: “Which suits those working full-time” is one link, but the passage is not built around causes and results.
whyNot.2: No problem is stated; the passage weighs two options rather than proposing a fix.

C.q: “When the Route 9 bridge closed for repairs, commuters switched to Oak Road. The extra traffic wore down Oak Road's surface, so potholes appeared within months. Those potholes, in turn, led to a sharp rise in tire-damage claims filed with the city.” Which best describes how the passage is organized?
options: as a problem followed by its fix
as a chain of causes and effects
as a comparison of two roads
as a description of the bridge
C.why: Each event causes the next: the closure shifts traffic, traffic creates potholes, potholes lead to claims. “So” and “led to” mark the links.

whyNot.0: The passage describes problems piling up; no fix is offered.
whyNot.2: Oak Road is not compared with the bridge on any feature; it is where the effects occur.
whyNot.3: The bridge's features are never described; its closure starts the chain.

C.q: A writer wants to explain, step by step, how a patient's prescription moves from the doctor's order to the pharmacy counter. Which organizational structure would best fit this purpose?
C.why: Explaining how something moves through a process, step by step, calls for sequence (chronological) order.

whyNot.1: There are not two things to compare; there is one process to follow.
whyNot.2: Classification sorts things into types; the writer is tracing steps.
whyNot.3: Order of importance ranks points to persuade; a process must follow its actual order.

reteach.title: Rooms in a house
reteach.question: Two houses can have the same rooms but different floor plans. A passage's facts are the rooms; its structure is the floor plan that connects them.

blocks.body: Take three facts about a flu season: vaccination rates fell, cases rose, and the clinic added Saturday hours. Arrange them by date and you have sequence. Link them with “because” and “so” and you have cause and effect. Open with “The problem was rising cases” and end with “The clinic's answer was Saturday hours,” and you have problem and solution. The facts stay put; the plan changes.

blocks.h: One set of facts, three plans
head: Floor plan
What connects the facts
rows: What went wrong and the fix

blocks.text: You find the floor plan by walking through the whole house, not by peeking into one room. Read all the connections before naming the structure.

explain.body: Narrative tells a story. Expository explains a topic with facts. Persuasive or argumentative argues a claim. Descriptive paints a subject with sensory detail. Technical gives steps, specifications and warnings.

test.q: A newspaper article reports that a new community clinic has opened, giving its location, hours, services and the number of staff hired. Which text type is it?
test.why: The article presents facts to explain a topic, the defining feature of expository writing.

whyNot.0: No story with characters and a plot is told.
whyNot.1: The article lists facts rather than painting the clinic in sensory detail.
whyNot.2: No claim is argued and no action is urged.

explain.body: Sequence arranges events or steps in time order (first, then, finally, dates). Cause and effect explains why something happened or what it led to (because, therefore, as a result, consequently, due to).

test.q: Which sentence uses a signal word that most clearly marks a cause-and-effect relationship?
options: Next, the nurse checked the patient's pulse.
Finally, the patient was moved to recovery.
The clinic closed; consequently, visits fell.
Unlike the old wing, the new wing has windows.
test.why: “Consequently” signals that the visits fell as a result of the closing: cause and effect.

whyNot.0: “Next” signals a step in a sequence.
whyNot.1: “Finally” signals the last step in a sequence.

explain.body: Compare and contrast shows likenesses and differences (similarly, both, however, unlike, whereas). Problem and solution names a difficulty and proposes or reports a fix (problem, issue, solve, propose).

test.q: “Night-shift nurses on Unit 5 reported trouble finding parking after 7 p.m. Hospital leaders proposed reserving the first two rows of Lot C for night staff, and the change began in May.” Which structure does the passage use?
test.why: A difficulty (no parking after 7 p.m.) is followed by a proposed and adopted fix (reserved rows).

whyNot.0: Nothing is compared; one problem and one response are described.
whyNot.2: No types or categories are defined.
whyNot.3: No points are ranked from least to most important.

explain.body: Description or spatial order moves through a place (above, beside, near, to the left). Order of importance ranks points (most important, above all). Classification sorts a subject into types or kinds, often defining each.

test.q: “At the center of the unit is the nurses' station. To its left, a short hallway leads to the medication room. Directly across from the station sit four patient rooms, and the supply closet is tucked behind them.” Which structure does the passage use?
test.why: The passage moves through a physical space using location words (at the center, to its left, across from, behind).

whyNot.0: No events happen in time order; the passage maps a place.
whyNot.1: The rooms are located, not sorted into categories.
whyNot.3: No room causes anything; the words show position.
